值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭示文革歷史的殘酷真相：深入了解1966年文化大革命初期，原本受人尊敬的中學教師如何一夕之間淪為階下囚與鬥爭對象。
  • 剖析極權政治對人性的扭曲：探討紅衛兵在政治狂熱下，如何從純真學生變成以荒誕藉口（如體態微胖、教授英文字詞）迫害師長的施暴者。
  • 警醒當代對「認同即和平」的迷思：藉由回顧歷史反思當前兩岸言論，深刻呈現極權體制下單純的身份認同並無法保障個人的尊嚴與安全。

摘要

引言：和平假象下的歷史警鐘

影片中，說書人阿牛哥針對台北第一女中教師區桂芝所言「台灣人就是中國人，承認了和平就會來」提出歷史反思。他指出，在中共體制下，「中國人」的身份從未保證過安全，教師這份職業也從不代表尊嚴。回顧1957年「反右運動」與1966年「文化大革命」，毛澤東發出「橫掃一切牛鬼蛇神」的號召，無數中學教師一夜之間從受人敬重的「心靈園丁」淪為階級敵人，甚至如北京師範大學附屬女子中學副校長卞仲耘，年僅五十歲便遭親手教導的女學生殘暴凌虐致死，遺體更被如垃圾般丟棄在宿舍外的板車旁。

荒謬的迫害：校園淪為人間煉獄

在文革初期的風暴中，處於知識分子底層、領取微薄薪資且行事低調的中學教師首當其衝。在階級鬥爭教育下成長的十幾歲紅衛兵，出於盲目的政治狂熱與殘酷好奇心，將鬥爭矛頭指向朝夕相處的恩師。校園裡鋪天蓋地的「大字報」羅織了各類荒誕罪名：政治老師提及「偉人也會犯錯」被控惡意攻擊領袖；英文老師板書「miss」與「mrs」被指企圖復辟資本主義；化學老師稱「化學重要」被質疑輕視毛澤東思想；甚至微胖身材被當作地主剝削的罪證，姓名與小說特務雷同便遭誣指通敵。隨之而來的是剃「陰陽頭」、掛黑牌遊街、皮帶鞭打與強灌污水，教師住所亦慘遭「抄家」，數十年的尊嚴與文明積累在革命狂潮中徹底崩毀。

從受害者到鬥爭工具：精神與良知的漫長凌遲

文革中後期，對教師的迫害由血腥肉體摧殘轉化為長期的精神凌遲。1967年中共號召「復課鬧革命」後，隨即推動大規模的「上山下鄉運動」，教師的角色隨之由「革命對象」轉化為「革命工具」，承擔動員學生前往農村的政治任務。面對貧困飢寒且毫無前途的真實農村，教師們被迫在講台上展露笑容，宣傳農村是「無比光榮」的前途，親手將天真的學子推入苦海。即便深知許多學生家庭遭遇重病與生計困難，但在動輒被扣上「反革命」帽子的恐怖氣氛下，無人敢提出異議，教師們被迫在體制逼迫下一步步出賣人性與教育良知。

================================================

Even a chemistry teacher could be. denounced just for saying chemistry was. important. How dare you claim chemistry. is important—is Mao Zedong Thought. not more important than chemistry? The. scariest part was that eventually, even. a person's appearance or name could. become "evidence" of a crime. One. overweight teacher was forced by. students to confess his history of " exploitation," the logic being: in the. old society, the working people. couldn't get enough to eat, so if. you're this fat, what else could you be. but a landlord? There was another. teacher who, just because his name. happened to be the same as a secret. agent in a novel, was accused of hiding. a radio at home and contacting Taiwan. every day. Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. Ge. Not long ago, Ou Guizi, a teacher. at Taipei First Girls High School, said. in an interview: "Taiwanese people are. Chinese. If we admit this, peace will. actually come." Many people hearing. this might think it's just a. pro-unification political stance. But. when I hear the word "peace," what. comes to mind isn't peace, but the. teachers forced onto struggle stages. during the Anti-Rightist Campaign and. the Cultural Revolution. In the minds. of many Taiwanese, teaching is a stable. and respectable profession. Most. teachers’ lifelong wish is just to. teach their classes well and guide. their students. Although many complain. that children are becoming harder to. teach, in Communist China, the identity. of being Chinese never guaranteed. safety, and the teaching profession. never represented dignity. Especially. in 1966, after Mao Zedong issued the. call to "sweep away all monsters and. demons," teachers across Communist. China went from being "gardeners of the. mind" to "monsters and demons" overnight. They were forced to wear. tall paper hats, have wooden signs hung. around their necks, faces smeared with. ink, and heads shaved in humiliating " yin-yang" styles. They were surrounded. by teenage Red Guards who punched and. kicked them. Most chilling of all,. these children attacking them had been. calling them "teacher" in the classroom. just a short while before. On August 5,. 1966, Bian Zhongyun, the deputy. principal of Beijing Normal University. Affiliated Girls 'Middle School, died. at the hands of her own students. She. was humiliated, beaten, and trampled. upon. By the time her family found her,. her body had been dumped like trash. next to a flatbed cart outside the. dormitory. Teacher Bian was only 50. years old that year. So today, I want. to join Teacher Ou Guizi in looking. back at this history and seeing what. you would have faced if you were a. middle school teacher in Communist. China. How you would be humiliated and. beaten by your own students, and how,. in that wave of fanaticism, your. dignity would be crushed step by step,. or even your life taken away. Let’s. start with how the CCP turned children. who were taught to respect teachers. into demons who humiliated them. When. many people think of the Cultural.

Revolution, they often picture the. high-ranking officials or famous. professors who were brought down. But. in reality, during the first wave of. impact after the revolution began, the. first to suffer were a group of. ordinary high school teachers. To be. fair, after the founding of the PRC,. high school teachers were actually at. the bottom of the intellectual. hierarchy. With a monthly salary of. fifty or sixty yuan, their lives were. neither wealthy nor prestigious. The. summer and winter breaks they once. enjoyed were filled with various. political study sessions, rural labor,. and socialist education movements. Most. of them were docile and knew how to. keep a low profile, having long since. learned to speak little and stay out of. the spotlight. Their only "privilege" was perhaps being able to read. internally circulated news in the. office. What they truly wanted was. simple: to stand at the podium, teach. their classes well, raise their. students, and live out their lives in. peace. Yet, no one expected that this. massive machine of the Cultural. Revolution would first swallow up this. group of the most humble and. defenseless people. In 1966, the slogan. "Sweep away all monsters and demons" echoed across the country, and Red. Guard rebel organizations sprouted. everywhere, composed of junior and. senior high school students. Some of. these children were thirteen or. fourteen, others seventeen or eighteen; many had not even reached adulthood. Some were in the classroom studying one. day, only to suddenly put on a red. armband the next, becoming. revolutionary vanguards. Having grown. up with an education centered on class. struggle, their understanding of the. world was simple: Chairman Mao is. forever great. Everything else is wrong. , and monsters and demons are hiding. right beside them. Thus, the childish,. blind fervor of youth, combined with a. bit of cruel curiosity, made these. young Red Guards eager to ferret out an. anti-party clique on campus to prove. their own revolutionary zeal. Their. familiar teachers naturally became the. easiest targets. It started with an. overwhelming tide of "big-character. posters." The content seems laughable. today, but back then, it could truly. cost you your life. A politics teacher. once said in class, "Everyone can make. mistakes, and great figures are no. exception." By the next day,. big-character posters covered the. campus: "Are you implying that Chairman. Mao can also make mistakes?""This is a. malicious attack on our great leader!" There was also an English teacher who. wrote the words "miss" and "mrs" on the. blackboard; students immediately rose. in anger: "We are a socialist country,. where do these' misses 'and' mrs 'come. from?""Are you trying to restore. capitalism?" Even a chemistry teacher. insisting that "chemistry is important" could be denounced: "How dare you say. chemistry is important? Is Mao Zedong. Thought not more important than. chemistry?" Most terrifyingly, later on.

, even a person's appearance or name. could become evidence of a crime. A. heavier-set teacher was forced by. students to confess to a history of. exploitation, for the absurd reason. that "In the old society, the working. people couldn't eat enough; if you're. this fat, what are you if not a. landlord?" Another teacher was accused. of hiding a radio transmitter at home. to contact Taiwan, simply because his. name happened to match that of a secret. agent in a novel. Once the floodgates. of violence were flung wide open, the. campus quickly turned into a living. hell. No laws were needed, nor were. investigations; a single word from the. Red Guards was enough to force the. once-gentle teachers to bow their heads. and stand at attention. They were hung. with heavy placards and forced to wear. tall dunce caps while being paraded. before the entire school. Some were. lashed with belts, some forced to kneel. , some pushed to the ground to crawl. like dogs, and others had their hair. shorn into humiliating "yin-yang" styles. They were mocked, and some were. even force-fed foul-smelling, filthy. sewage water. Youth should have been. filled with sunshine, but in that. peculiar era, youth ignited by. political fanaticism ultimately turned. into total destruction. Teachers' homes. were thoroughly ransacked. Everything. accumulated over half a lifetime—. books, paintings, albums, even pots and. quilts—was turned over, smashed, or. stolen. There were no lists or receipts. , and many families lost everything. overnight. Yesterday they were reading. Tang poetry in the classroom; today. they were being held down and cursed. Yesterday they were teaching students. how to be decent human beings; today. they were being trampled underfoot. It. wasn't just physical pain; it was the. shattering of everything a person had. believed in their whole life—. knowledge, education, sentiment,. civilization, and kindness—all torn. to pieces in a few days by sharp belts. and loud slaps in the name of. revolution. Next, let's discuss why. teachers were both the targets and the. tools of the revolution. If the. persecution of teachers in the early. stages of the revolution was a bloody,. frenzied slash, then by the mid-to-late. Cultural Revolution, this disaster had. become a rusty, dull knife, slicing. away at everyone—a long, seemingly. endless form of mental torture. On. October 14, 1967, Mao Zedong issued a. notice calling for the resumption of. classes to carry out the revolution. Although teachers were no longer being. beaten at this point, they fell into. another, more painful abyss, forced to. betray their humanity little by little. every day, losing their dignity inch by. inch. One year later, Mao issued a call. for educated youth to go to the. countryside, changing the fate of. countless families forever. Teachers. shifted from being targets of the. revolution to tools of the revolution,. receiving the "glorious" political task. of mobilizing students to head up to. the mountains and down to the.

countryside. This was a truly cruel. reality, for the countryside was not. the romanticized place the CCP. propaganda depicted; it was not a "vast. horizon" where one could make a great. impact, but a place of poverty, hunger,. cold, exhaustion, and a life with no. future. Yet, teachers had to stand on. the podium, put on their brightest,. most radiant smiles, and tell the young. , innocent faces below, "Students, go. to the countryside, go to the frontier; that is the most glorious revolutionary. path." Some students truly had. difficulties at home—parents were. critically ill, siblings were young,. and there was no labor force—teachers. knew this, and the neighborhood. committees knew it too, but who dared. to say they wouldn't go? Once you. refused, you would immediately be. labeled a counter-revolutionary. opposing Chairman Mao, and thus, a. ridiculous campaign to force people. into the countryside swept across the. occupied areas. Parents were summoned. to "study sessions," which, despite the. name, were essentially a form of house. arrest. Work units took turns sending. people to stand guard, forbidding them. from working or returning home; the. sessions would only end once their. children had signed up to go to the. countryside. Most absurd were the. propaganda teams who would bang gongs. and drums at the entrances of apartment. buildings, shouting, "Going to the. mountains and countryside is glorious!" One group would finish, and another. would take over, shouting until. midnight; many parents collapsed under. this mental torture. Teachers were. caught in the middle of all this. They. knew full well that these methods were. inhumane, yet they were forced to carry. them out, for if they failed their. quota, the propaganda teams would. question their class stance. However,. those with true influence or. connections didn't need teachers to. persuade them at all. With a mysterious. phone call or a slip of paper bearing a. red seal, the files of cadres 'children. were quietly whisked away in the dead. of night; they didn't need to go to the. countryside because they had already. been moved into the military,. government units, or the city's best. factories. In the end, those stuffed. into green-skinned trains and sent to. the Great Northern Wilderness of. Heilongjiang, the grasslands of Inner. Mongolia, or the Yunnan Production and. Construction Corps were all children of. ordinary folks with no connections. Thus, the most ironic scene of the. Cultural Revolution emerged: teachers. were both victims and perpetrators. The. entire education system became an. absurd stage where teachers were no. longer teachers, students no longer. students, and schools no longer schools. —they were both the targets and the. tools of the revolution. While being " re-educated," they still had to act as. the pulse of the movement. They were. like a group of people swept into the. mud by a flood; unable to stand up and. unable to escape, they could only watch. helplessly as they sank deeper into the.

mire, awaiting their demise. Next,. let’s talk about what the Cultural. Revolution truly destroyed. If you ask. me, A-Niu, what the Cultural Revolution. really destroyed, my answer is: the. human soul. The profession of teaching. is much like a candle, consuming itself. to light the way for others, especially. for middle school teachers. They are. not like university professors who can. leave behind scholarly achievements,. nor are they like scientists capable of. earth-shattering inventions. For many. middle school teachers, their greatest. life achievement is watching their. students grow up. "Students everywhere" is not just a polite phrase; it was the. true spiritual pillar that sustained. many teachers amidst the drudgery of. daily life. But suddenly, the. revolution arrived, and this spiritual. pillar was forcibly snapped by the era. Many teachers recalled later that what. truly broke them was never the whips or. the slaps, but when you were kneeling. on the playground, struggling to lift. your head, only to see the student you. loved and cherished most standing in. the front row, a look of sacred. fanaticism on their face, screaming at. you, "Down with the reactionary. academic authority!" In that instant,. the last remnants of humanity and hope. within the teacher’s heart snapped. with a clean break. From then on, many. people never again believed that. education could change a person. For. the next ten years, they watched as. batch after batch of students left. school—not for universities, but for. the frontier. To the countryside and. farms; as the trains pulled away, so. did the youth of a generation. By the. era of workers, peasants, and soldiers. attending university, the standard for. admission was not grades, but class. background. Thus, classrooms in. university Chinese departments were. filled with students who couldn't even. write a letter home properly or grasp. basic punctuation. Because their. political backgrounds were "correct," they were recommended for university by. communes, factories, and military units. . In the Northeast, a candidate named. Zhang Tiesheng took the college. entrance exam, handed in a blank paper. for physics and chemistry, but wrote a. letter on the back of the test paper. claiming he had no time to review. because he was laboring in the. countryside. As a result, he became a " hero of the blank paper" idolized by. the entire nation. This absurdity. quickly became the norm in all. universities across Communist China,. while truly talented youths who loved. to read were, at that very moment,. stuck in pigsties in the countryside or. carrying hoes to clear wasteland. It. wasn't that the teachers didn't. understand; they just couldn't speak,. because in that era, the truth itself. was dangerous. Therefore, during the. Cultural Revolution, many, many people. died from violence, but even more died. from long-term humiliation and. psychological erosion, especially the. teachers. Because the profession of. teaching relies most on believing—.

believing in knowledge, believing in. honesty, and believing that education. can make people better. Yet, the. cruelest aspect of the CCP is that it. forced teachers to personally destroy. all of this. They were driven by the. revolution to betray their conscience,. to tell lies, to negate knowledge, and. to destroy everything they once. cherished most. In the end, many. teachers survived, but they no longer. believed in education, nor did they. believe in the human heart. Some, when. speaking of the Cultural Revolution in. their later years, would simply remark. that back then, we weren't teaching; we. were learning how to survive. Finally,. is today's occupied territory truly. different? Whenever I bring up the dark. history of the CCP, people comment that. it’s a different era now, and things. are nothing like they used to be. Yes,. you are right; today’s occupied. territory no longer carries out the. Cultural Revolution. Teachers are not. paraded with heavy wooden signs around. their necks, nor are their heads shaved. into "yin-yang" cuts for a slip of the. tongue while kneeling on burning. cinders, nor are they beaten to death. by their own students as class enemies. Yet today, if you walk into those. campuses guarded by strict access. controls and facial recognition, you. will find that many fundamental things. have never actually changed. 摘要

引言：和平假象下的歷史警鐘

影片中，說書人阿牛哥針對台北第一女中教師區桂芝所言「台灣人就是中國人，承認了和平就會來」提出歷史反思。他指出，在中共體制下，「中國人」的身份從未保證過安全，教師這份職業也從不代表尊嚴。回顧1957年「反右運動」與1966年「文化大革命」，毛澤東發出「橫掃一切牛鬼蛇神」的號召，無數中學教師一夜之間從受人敬重的「心靈園丁」淪為階級敵人，甚至如北京師範大學附屬女子中學副校長卞仲耘，年僅五十歲便遭親手教導的女學生殘暴凌虐致死，遺體更被如垃圾般丟棄在宿舍外的板車旁。

荒謬的迫害：校園淪為人間煉獄

在文革初期的風暴中，處於知識分子底層、領取微薄薪資且行事低調的中學教師首當其衝。在階級鬥爭教育下成長的十幾歲紅衛兵，出於盲目的政治狂熱與殘酷好奇心，將鬥爭矛頭指向朝夕相處的恩師。校園裡鋪天蓋地的「大字報」羅織了各類荒誕罪名：政治老師提及「偉人也會犯錯」被控惡意攻擊領袖；英文老師板書「miss」與「mrs」被指企圖復辟資本主義；化學老師稱「化學重要」被質疑輕視毛澤東思想；甚至微胖身材被當作地主剝削的罪證，姓名與小說特務雷同便遭誣指通敵。隨之而來的是剃「陰陽頭」、掛黑牌遊街、皮帶鞭打與強灌污水，教師住所亦慘遭「抄家」，數十年的尊嚴與文明積累在革命狂潮中徹底崩毀。

從受害者到鬥爭工具：精神與良知的漫長凌遲

文革中後期，對教師的迫害由血腥肉體摧殘轉化為長期的精神凌遲。1967年中共號召「復課鬧革命」後，隨即推動大規模的「上山下鄉運動」，教師的角色隨之由「革命對象」轉化為「革命工具」，承擔動員學生前往農村的政治任務。面對貧困飢寒且毫無前途的真實農村，教師們被迫在講台上展露笑容，宣傳農村是「無比光榮」的前途，親手將天真的學子推入苦海。即便深知許多學生家庭遭遇重病與生計困難，但在動輒被扣上「反革命」帽子的恐怖氣氛下，無人敢提出異議，教師們被迫在體制逼迫下一步步出賣人性與教育良知。

Even a chemistry teacher could be. denounced just for saying chemistry was. important. How dare you claim chemistry. is important—is Mao Zedong Thought. not more important than chemistry? The. scariest part was that eventually, even. a person's appearance or name could. become "evidence" of a crime. In the minds. of many Taiwanese, teaching is a stable. and respectable profession. Most. teachers’ lifelong wish is just to. teach their classes well and guide. their students. Although many complain. that children are becoming harder to. teach, in Communist China, the identity. of being Chinese never guaranteed. safety, and the teaching profession. never represented dignity. Especially. in 1966, after Mao Zedong issued the. call to "sweep away all monsters and. demons," teachers across Communist. China went from being "gardeners of the. mind" to "monsters and demons" overnight. Teacher Bian was only 50. years old that year. So today, I want. to join Teacher Ou Guizi in looking. back at this history and seeing what. you would have faced if you were a. middle school teacher in Communist. China. How you would be humiliated and. beaten by your own students, and how,. in that wave of fanaticism, your. dignity would be crushed step by step,. or even your life taken away. Let’s. start with how the CCP turned children. who were taught to respect teachers. into demons who humiliated them. When. many people think of the Cultural.

Revolution, they often picture the. high-ranking officials or famous. professors who were brought down. But. in reality, during the first wave of. impact after the revolution began, the. first to suffer were a group of. ordinary high school teachers. To be. fair, after the founding of the PRC,. high school teachers were actually at. the bottom of the intellectual. hierarchy. With a monthly salary of. fifty or sixty yuan, their lives were. neither wealthy nor prestigious. The. summer and winter breaks they once. enjoyed were filled with various. political study sessions, rural labor,. and socialist education movements. Most. of them were docile and knew how to. keep a low profile, having long since. learned to speak little and stay out of. the spotlight. Their only "privilege" was perhaps being able to read. internally circulated news in the. office. What they truly wanted was. simple: to stand at the podium, teach. their classes well, raise their. students, and live out their lives in. peace. Yet, no one expected that this. massive machine of the Cultural. Revolution would first swallow up this. group of the most humble and. defenseless people. In 1966, the slogan. "Sweep away all monsters and demons" echoed across the country, and Red. Guard rebel organizations sprouted. everywhere, composed of junior and. senior high school students. Some of. these children were thirteen or. fourteen, others seventeen or eighteen; many had not even reached adulthood. Some were in the classroom studying one. day, only to suddenly put on a red. armband the next, becoming. revolutionary vanguards. Having grown. up with an education centered on class. struggle, their understanding of the. world was simple: Chairman Mao is. forever great. Everything else is wrong. , and monsters and demons are hiding. right beside them. Thus, the childish,. blind fervor of youth, combined with a. bit of cruel curiosity, made these. young Red Guards eager to ferret out an. anti-party clique on campus to prove. their own revolutionary zeal. Their. familiar teachers naturally became the. easiest targets. It started with an. overwhelming tide of "big-character. posters." The content seems laughable. today, but back then, it could truly. cost you your life. A politics teacher. once said in class, "Everyone can make. mistakes, and great figures are no. exception." Once the floodgates. of violence were flung wide open, the. campus quickly turned into a living. hell. No laws were needed, nor were. investigations; a single word from the. Red Guards was enough to force the. once-gentle teachers to bow their heads. and stand at attention. They were hung. with heavy placards and forced to wear. tall dunce caps while being paraded. before the entire school. Some were. lashed with belts, some forced to kneel. , some pushed to the ground to crawl. like dogs, and others had their hair. shorn into humiliating "yin-yang" styles. They were mocked, and some were. even force-fed foul-smelling, filthy. sewage water. Youth should have been. filled with sunshine, but in that. peculiar era, youth ignited by. political fanaticism ultimately turned. into total destruction. Teachers' homes. were thoroughly ransacked. Everything. accumulated over half a lifetime—. books, paintings, albums, even pots and. quilts—was turned over, smashed, or. stolen. There were no lists or receipts. , and many families lost everything. overnight. Yesterday they were reading. Tang poetry in the classroom; today. they were being held down and cursed. Yesterday they were teaching students. how to be decent human beings; today. they were being trampled underfoot. It. wasn't just physical pain; it was the. shattering of everything a person had. believed in their whole life—. knowledge, education, sentiment,. civilization, and kindness—all torn. to pieces in a few days by sharp belts. and loud slaps in the name of. revolution. Next, let's discuss why. teachers were both the targets and the. tools of the revolution. If the. persecution of teachers in the early. stages of the revolution was a bloody,. frenzied slash, then by the mid-to-late. Cultural Revolution, this disaster had. become a rusty, dull knife, slicing. away at everyone—a long, seemingly. endless form of mental torture. On. October 14, 1967, Mao Zedong issued a. notice calling for the resumption of. classes to carry out the revolution. Although teachers were no longer being. beaten at this point, they fell into. another, more painful abyss, forced to. betray their humanity little by little. every day, losing their dignity inch by. inch. One year later, Mao issued a call. for educated youth to go to the. countryside, changing the fate of. countless families forever. Teachers. shifted from being targets of the. revolution to tools of the revolution,. receiving the "glorious" political task. of mobilizing students to head up to. the mountains and down to the.

countryside. This was a truly cruel. reality, for the countryside was not. the romanticized place the CCP. propaganda depicted; it was not a "vast. horizon" where one could make a great. impact, but a place of poverty, hunger,. cold, exhaustion, and a life with no. future. Yet, teachers had to stand on. the podium, put on their brightest,. most radiant smiles, and tell the young. , innocent faces below, "Students, go. to the countryside, go to the frontier; that is the most glorious revolutionary. path." Some students truly had. difficulties at home—parents were. critically ill, siblings were young,. and there was no labor force—teachers. knew this, and the neighborhood. committees knew it too, but who dared. to say they wouldn't go? Once you. refused, you would immediately be. labeled a counter-revolutionary. opposing Chairman Mao, and thus, a. ridiculous campaign to force people. into the countryside swept across the. occupied areas. Parents were summoned. to "study sessions," which, despite the. name, were essentially a form of house. arrest. Work units took turns sending. people to stand guard, forbidding them. from working or returning home; the. sessions would only end once their. children had signed up to go to the. countryside. Most absurd were the. propaganda teams who would bang gongs. and drums at the entrances of apartment. buildings, shouting, "Going to the. mountains and countryside is glorious!" One group would finish, and another. would take over, shouting until. midnight; many parents collapsed under. this mental torture. Teachers were. caught in the middle of all this. They. knew full well that these methods were. inhumane, yet they were forced to carry. them out, for if they failed their. quota, the propaganda teams would. question their class stance. However,. those with true influence or. connections didn't need teachers to. persuade them at all. With a mysterious. phone call or a slip of paper bearing a. red seal, the files of cadres 'children. were quietly whisked away in the dead. of night; they didn't need to go to the. countryside because they had already. been moved into the military,. government units, or the city's best. factories. In the end, those stuffed. into green-skinned trains and sent to. the Great Northern Wilderness of. Heilongjiang, the grasslands of Inner. Mongolia, or the Yunnan Production and. Construction Corps were all children of. ordinary folks with no connections. Thus, the most ironic scene of the. Cultural Revolution emerged: teachers. were both victims and perpetrators. The. entire education system became an. absurd stage where teachers were no. longer teachers, students no longer. students, and schools no longer schools. —they were both the targets and the. tools of the revolution. While being " re-educated," they still had to act as. the pulse of the movement. They were. like a group of people swept into the. mud by a flood; unable to stand up and. unable to escape, they could only watch. helplessly as they sank deeper into the.

mire, awaiting their demise. Next,. let’s talk about what the Cultural. Revolution truly destroyed. If you ask. me, A-Niu, what the Cultural Revolution. really destroyed, my answer is: the. human soul. The profession of teaching. is much like a candle, consuming itself. to light the way for others, especially. for middle school teachers. They are. not like university professors who can. leave behind scholarly achievements,. nor are they like scientists capable of. earth-shattering inventions. For many. middle school teachers, their greatest. life achievement is watching their. students grow up. "Students everywhere" is not just a polite phrase; it was the. true spiritual pillar that sustained. many teachers amidst the drudgery of. daily life. But suddenly, the. revolution arrived, and this spiritual. pillar was forcibly snapped by the era. Many teachers recalled later that what. truly broke them was never the whips or. the slaps, but when you were kneeling. on the playground, struggling to lift. your head, only to see the student you. loved and cherished most standing in. the front row, a look of sacred. fanaticism on their face, screaming at. you, "Down with the reactionary. academic authority!" In that instant,. the last remnants of humanity and hope. within the teacher’s heart snapped. with a clean break. From then on, many. people never again believed that. education could change a person. For. the next ten years, they watched as. batch after batch of students left. school—not for universities, but for. the frontier. To the countryside and. farms; as the trains pulled away, so. did the youth of a generation. By the. era of workers, peasants, and soldiers. attending university, the standard for. admission was not grades, but class. background. Because their. political backgrounds were "correct," they were recommended for university by. communes, factories, and military units. . In the Northeast, a candidate named. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭示文革歷史的殘酷真相：深入了解1966年文化大革命初期，原本受人尊敬的中學教師如何一夕之間淪為階下囚與鬥爭對象。
  • 剖析極權政治對人性的扭曲：探討紅衛兵在政治狂熱下，如何從純真學生變成以荒誕藉口（如體態微胖、教授英文字詞）迫害師長的施暴者。
  • 警醒當代對「認同即和平」的迷思：藉由回顧歷史反思當前兩岸言論，深刻呈現極權體制下單純的身份認同並無法保障個人的尊嚴與安全。

摘要

引言：和平假象下的歷史警鐘

影片中，說書人阿牛哥針對台北第一女中教師區桂芝所言「台灣人就是中國人，承認了和平就會來」提出歷史反思。他指出，在中共體制下，「中國人」的身份從未保證過安全，教師這份職業也從不代表尊嚴。回顧1957年「反右運動」與1966年「文化大革命」，毛澤東發出「橫掃一切牛鬼蛇神」的號召，無數中學教師一夜之間從受人敬重的「心靈園丁」淪為階級敵人，甚至如北京師範大學附屬女子中學副校長卞仲耘，年僅五十歲便遭親手教導的女學生殘暴凌虐致死，遺體更被如垃圾般丟棄在宿舍外的板車旁。

荒謬的迫害：校園淪為人間煉獄

在文革初期的風暴中，處於知識分子底層、領取微薄薪資且行事低調的中學教師首當其衝。在階級鬥爭教育下成長的十幾歲紅衛兵，出於盲目的政治狂熱與殘酷好奇心，將鬥爭矛頭指向朝夕相處的恩師。校園裡鋪天蓋地的「大字報」羅織了各類荒誕罪名：政治老師提及「偉人也會犯錯」被控惡意攻擊領袖；英文老師板書「miss」與「mrs」被指企圖復辟資本主義；化學老師稱「化學重要」被質疑輕視毛澤東思想；甚至微胖身材被當作地主剝削的罪證，姓名與小說特務雷同便遭誣指通敵。隨之而來的是剃「陰陽頭」、掛黑牌遊街、皮帶鞭打與強灌污水，教師住所亦慘遭「抄家」，數十年的尊嚴與文明積累在革命狂潮中徹底崩毀。

從受害者到鬥爭工具：精神與良知的漫長凌遲

文革中後期，對教師的迫害由血腥肉體摧殘轉化為長期的精神凌遲。1967年中共號召「復課鬧革命」後，隨即推動大規模的「上山下鄉運動」，教師的角色隨之由「革命對象」轉化為「革命工具」，承擔動員學生前往農村的政治任務。面對貧困飢寒且毫無前途的真實農村，教師們被迫在講台上展露笑容，宣傳農村是「無比光榮」的前途，親手將天真的學子推入苦海。即便深知許多學生家庭遭遇重病與生計困難，但在動輒被扣上「反革命」帽子的恐怖氣氛下，無人敢提出異議，教師們被迫在體制逼迫下一步步出賣人性與教育良知。

================================================

Even a chemistry teacher could be. denounced just for saying chemistry was. important. How dare you claim chemistry. is important—is Mao Zedong Thought. not more important than chemistry? The. scariest part was that eventually, even. a person's appearance or name could. become "evidence" of a crime. One. overweight teacher was forced by. students to confess his history of " exploitation," the logic being: in the. old society, the working people. couldn't get enough to eat, so if. you're this fat, what else could you be. but a landlord? There was another. teacher who, just because his name. happened to be the same as a secret. agent in a novel, was accused of hiding. a radio at home and contacting Taiwan. every day. Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. Ge. Not long ago, Ou Guizi, a teacher. at Taipei First Girls High School, said. in an interview: "Taiwanese people are. Chinese. If we admit this, peace will. actually come." Many people hearing. this might think it's just a. pro-unification political stance. But. when I hear the word "peace," what. comes to mind isn't peace, but the. teachers forced onto struggle stages. during the Anti-Rightist Campaign and. the Cultural Revolution. In the minds. of many Taiwanese, teaching is a stable. and respectable profession. Most. teachers’ lifelong wish is just to. teach their classes well and guide. their students. Although many complain. that children are becoming harder to. teach, in Communist China, the identity. of being Chinese never guaranteed. safety, and the teaching profession. never represented dignity. Especially. in 1966, after Mao Zedong issued the. call to "sweep away all monsters and. demons," teachers across Communist. China went from being "gardeners of the. mind" to "monsters and demons" overnight. They were forced to wear. tall paper hats, have wooden signs hung. around their necks, faces smeared with. ink, and heads shaved in humiliating " yin-yang" styles. They were surrounded. by teenage Red Guards who punched and. kicked them. Most chilling of all,. these children attacking them had been. calling them "teacher" in the classroom. just a short while before. On August 5,. 1966, Bian Zhongyun, the deputy. principal of Beijing Normal University. Affiliated Girls 'Middle School, died. at the hands of her own students. She. was humiliated, beaten, and trampled. upon. By the time her family found her,. her body had been dumped like trash. next to a flatbed cart outside the. dormitory. Teacher Bian was only 50. years old that year. So today, I want. to join Teacher Ou Guizi in looking. back at this history and seeing what. you would have faced if you were a. middle school teacher in Communist. China. How you would be humiliated and. beaten by your own students, and how,. in that wave of fanaticism, your. dignity would be crushed step by step,. or even your life taken away. Let’s. start with how the CCP turned children. who were taught to respect teachers. into demons who humiliated them. When. many people think of the Cultural.

Revolution, they often picture the. high-ranking officials or famous. professors who were brought down. But. in reality, during the first wave of. impact after the revolution began, the. first to suffer were a group of. ordinary high school teachers. To be. fair, after the founding of the PRC,. high school teachers were actually at. the bottom of the intellectual. hierarchy. With a monthly salary of. fifty or sixty yuan, their lives were. neither wealthy nor prestigious. The. summer and winter breaks they once. enjoyed were filled with various. political study sessions, rural labor,. and socialist education movements. Most. of them were docile and knew how to. keep a low profile, having long since. learned to speak little and stay out of. the spotlight. Their only "privilege" was perhaps being able to read. internally circulated news in the. office. What they truly wanted was. simple: to stand at the podium, teach. their classes well, raise their. students, and live out their lives in. peace. Yet, no one expected that this. massive machine of the Cultural. Revolution would first swallow up this. group of the most humble and. defenseless people. In 1966, the slogan. "Sweep away all monsters and demons" echoed across the country, and Red. Guard rebel organizations sprouted. everywhere, composed of junior and. senior high school students. Some of. these children were thirteen or. fourteen, others seventeen or eighteen; many had not even reached adulthood. Some were in the classroom studying one. day, only to suddenly put on a red. armband the next, becoming. revolutionary vanguards. Having grown. up with an education centered on class. struggle, their understanding of the. world was simple: Chairman Mao is. forever great. Everything else is wrong. , and monsters and demons are hiding. right beside them. Thus, the childish,. blind fervor of youth, combined with a. bit of cruel curiosity, made these. young Red Guards eager to ferret out an. anti-party clique on campus to prove. their own revolutionary zeal. Their. familiar teachers naturally became the. easiest targets. It started with an. overwhelming tide of "big-character. posters." The content seems laughable. today, but back then, it could truly. cost you your life. A politics teacher. once said in class, "Everyone can make. mistakes, and great figures are no. exception." By the next day,. big-character posters covered the. campus: "Are you implying that Chairman. Mao can also make mistakes?""This is a. malicious attack on our great leader!" There was also an English teacher who. wrote the words "miss" and "mrs" on the. blackboard; students immediately rose. in anger: "We are a socialist country,. where do these' misses 'and' mrs 'come. from?""Are you trying to restore. capitalism?" Even a chemistry teacher. insisting that "chemistry is important" could be denounced: "How dare you say. chemistry is important? Is Mao Zedong. Thought not more important than. chemistry?" Most terrifyingly, later on.

, even a person's appearance or name. could become evidence of a crime. A. heavier-set teacher was forced by. students to confess to a history of. exploitation, for the absurd reason. that "In the old society, the working. people couldn't eat enough; if you're. this fat, what are you if not a. landlord?" Another teacher was accused. of hiding a radio transmitter at home. to contact Taiwan, simply because his. name happened to match that of a secret. agent in a novel. Once the floodgates. of violence were flung wide open, the. campus quickly turned into a living. hell. No laws were needed, nor were. investigations; a single word from the. Red Guards was enough to force the. once-gentle teachers to bow their heads. and stand at attention. They were hung. with heavy placards and forced to wear. tall dunce caps while being paraded. before the entire school. Some were. lashed with belts, some forced to kneel. , some pushed to the ground to crawl. like dogs, and others had their hair. shorn into humiliating "yin-yang" styles. They were mocked, and some were. even force-fed foul-smelling, filthy. sewage water. Youth should have been. filled with sunshine, but in that. peculiar era, youth ignited by. political fanaticism ultimately turned. into total destruction. Teachers' homes. were thoroughly ransacked. Everything. accumulated over half a lifetime—. books, paintings, albums, even pots and. quilts—was turned over, smashed, or. stolen. There were no lists or receipts. , and many families lost everything. overnight. Yesterday they were reading. Tang poetry in the classroom; today. they were being held down and cursed. Yesterday they were teaching students. how to be decent human beings; today. they were being trampled underfoot. It. wasn't just physical pain; it was the. shattering of everything a person had. believed in their whole life—. knowledge, education, sentiment,. civilization, and kindness—all torn. to pieces in a few days by sharp belts. and loud slaps in the name of. revolution. Next, let's discuss why. teachers were both the targets and the. tools of the revolution. If the. persecution of teachers in the early. stages of the revolution was a bloody,. frenzied slash, then by the mid-to-late. Cultural Revolution, this disaster had. become a rusty, dull knife, slicing. away at everyone—a long, seemingly. endless form of mental torture. On. October 14, 1967, Mao Zedong issued a. notice calling for the resumption of. classes to carry out the revolution. Although teachers were no longer being. beaten at this point, they fell into. another, more painful abyss, forced to. betray their humanity little by little. every day, losing their dignity inch by. inch. One year later, Mao issued a call. for educated youth to go to the. countryside, changing the fate of. countless families forever. Teachers. shifted from being targets of the. revolution to tools of the revolution,. receiving the "glorious" political task. of mobilizing students to head up to. the mountains and down to the.

countryside. This was a truly cruel. reality, for the countryside was not. the romanticized place the CCP. propaganda depicted; it was not a "vast. horizon" where one could make a great. impact, but a place of poverty, hunger,. cold, exhaustion, and a life with no. future. Yet, teachers had to stand on. the podium, put on their brightest,. most radiant smiles, and tell the young. , innocent faces below, "Students, go. to the countryside, go to the frontier; that is the most glorious revolutionary. path." Some students truly had. difficulties at home—parents were. critically ill, siblings were young,. and there was no labor force—teachers. knew this, and the neighborhood. committees knew it too, but who dared. to say they wouldn't go? Once you. refused, you would immediately be. labeled a counter-revolutionary. opposing Chairman Mao, and thus, a. ridiculous campaign to force people. into the countryside swept across the. occupied areas. Parents were summoned. to "study sessions," which, despite the. name, were essentially a form of house. arrest. Work units took turns sending. people to stand guard, forbidding them. from working or returning home; the. sessions would only end once their. children had signed up to go to the. countryside. Most absurd were the. propaganda teams who would bang gongs. and drums at the entrances of apartment. buildings, shouting, "Going to the. mountains and countryside is glorious!" One group would finish, and another. would take over, shouting until. midnight; many parents collapsed under. this mental torture. Teachers were. caught in the middle of all this. They. knew full well that these methods were. inhumane, yet they were forced to carry. them out, for if they failed their. quota, the propaganda teams would. question their class stance. However,. those with true influence or. connections didn't need teachers to. persuade them at all. With a mysterious. phone call or a slip of paper bearing a. red seal, the files of cadres 'children. were quietly whisked away in the dead. of night; they didn't need to go to the. countryside because they had already. been moved into the military,. government units, or the city's best. factories. In the end, those stuffed. into green-skinned trains and sent to. the Great Northern Wilderness of. Heilongjiang, the grasslands of Inner. Mongolia, or the Yunnan Production and. Construction Corps were all children of. ordinary folks with no connections. Thus, the most ironic scene of the. Cultural Revolution emerged: teachers. were both victims and perpetrators. The. entire education system became an. absurd stage where teachers were no. longer teachers, students no longer. students, and schools no longer schools. —they were both the targets and the. tools of the revolution. While being " re-educated," they still had to act as. the pulse of the movement. They were. like a group of people swept into the. mud by a flood; unable to stand up and. unable to escape, they could only watch. helplessly as they sank deeper into the.

mire, awaiting their demise. Next,. let’s talk about what the Cultural. Revolution truly destroyed. If you ask. me, A-Niu, what the Cultural Revolution. really destroyed, my answer is: the. human soul.
